title: Attack and defend: reconnaissance and port scans
blurb: Recognize a port scan in flow data and IPS events, then shrink what the scan can find on an edge router.
scenario: Secure Network Analytics flags one outside address touching hundreds of ports on your public range in a few seconds. Reconnaissance usually comes before an attack, so read the signs, tune detection on the FTD, and reduce what the edge exposes.
topology:
Internet ── R-EDGE ── FTD ── DMZ servers
   Secure Network Analytics collects NetFlow from R-EDGE
objectives: Tell scan types apart from their flow records
Turn off services the edge router doesn't need
Filter management access at the edge

steps.title: Read the flows
steps.learn: Scans leave clear patterns in flow data. A **horizontal scan** hits one port on many hosts, looking for a single service. A **vertical scan** hits many ports on one host, mapping everything it runs. A **SYN (half-open) scan** sends SYNs and never completes the handshake, so flows show a SYN with an RST or no reply and almost no bytes.
steps.task: Match each flow pattern to the scan type it shows.

steps.title: Detect scans on the FTD
steps.learn: On FTD, **Threat Detection** in the network analysis policy watches for portscans. You pick which **protocols** to watch, which **scan types** to detect, and a **sensitivity**. Higher sensitivity catches slower scans but raises more false alarms. With the IPS rules for portscan events enabled, the events show up in FMC.
steps.task: Turn on portscan detection for **TCP** and **UDP**, detect **all scan types**, use **medium** sensitivity, and set the action to **generate events**.
steps.screen: FMC: Policies › Access Control › Threat Detection

steps.title: Shrink the attack surface
steps.learn: Every service a device runs is something a scan can find. Turn off what you don't use: the **HTTP server**, **CDP** on the Internet-facing interface (it reveals the model and IOS version), and **ICMP unreachables** and **redirects** on that interface, which help scanners map the network.
steps.task: Turn off the HTTP and HTTPS servers. On **GigabitEthernet0/0** (outside), turn off CDP, ICMP unreachables and ICMP redirects.
steps.hint: `no ip http server`, `no ip http secure-server`, `interface g0/0`, `no cdp enable`, `no ip unreachables`, `no ip redirects`.

commands.note: CDP stays on for internal interfaces, where it's useful.

steps.title: Hide management from the Internet
steps.learn: Even with SSH only, the management port should answer just your admins. An **access-class** on the VTY lines drops everyone else, so a scan sees nothing listening.
steps.task: Create standard ACL **VTY-ADMINS** permitting **10.10.99.0/24**, and apply it inbound on **VTY lines 0 4**.
steps.hint: `ip access-list standard VTY-ADMINS`, `permit 10.10.99.0 0.0.0.255`, `line vty 0 4`, `access-class VTY-ADMINS in`.

steps.title: Check what's left
steps.task: Show which TCP ports the router is still listening on.

commands.output:
Active internet connections (servers and established)
Prot        Local Address      Foreign Address     Service    State
 tcp                 *:22                  *:0     SSH-Server   LISTEN
commands.note: Only SSH remains, and the VTY ACL limits who can reach it.

steps.title: Why it matters
steps.question: Why is detecting a scan useful even though a scan alone does no damage?

options.text: Reconnaissance is an early kill-chain stage. Spotting it gives warning of a likely attack and names a source to watch or block.
Scans crash routers, so they must be blocked.
options.why: Ordinary scans don't crash anything. Their value to an attacker is information.

options.text: It isn't useful. Scans are too common to matter.
options.why: Most are background noise, but a targeted scan followed by exploit attempts is a strong signal.

summary: Horizontal, vertical and SYN scans in flow data, FTD portscan detection, turning off unused edge services (HTTP, CDP, unreachables, redirects), a VTY access-class, and checking open ports.
